questions.enonce_markdown:
Using the following terms: "G.C.E Examiner" as the major term, "Pedagogues" as minor term and "chiefs" as the middle term respectively:
(i) Construct an AEE-2 syllogism and an EAO-3 syllogism. (3 x 2 marks)
(ii) State the mood names in a(i) above. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P$ = G.C.E Examiners (major term), $S$ = pedagogues (minor term), $M$ = chiefs (middle term). In figure 2 the middle term is the predicate of both premises; in figure 3 it is the subject of both premises.

**(i) The two syllogisms.**

*AEE-2* (major premise A, minor premise E, conclusion E, figure 2):

> All G.C.E Examiners are chiefs. (All $P$ are $M$)
> No pedagogues are chiefs. (No $S$ are $M$)
> Therefore, no pedagogues are G.C.E Examiners. (No $S$ are $P$)

*EAO-3* (major premise E, minor premise A, conclusion O, figure 3):

> No chiefs are G.C.E Examiners. (No $M$ are $P$)
> All chiefs are pedagogues. (All $M$ are $S$)
> Therefore, some pedagogues are not G.C.E Examiners. (Some $S$ are not $P$)

**(ii) Mood names.**

- AEE-2 is **Camestres** (the mnemonic of figure 2: Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco).
- EAO-3 is **Felapton** (the mnemonic of figure 3: Darapti, Disamis, Datisi, Felapton, Bocardo, Ferison).

Both are valid moods of the traditional classification (Felapton on the traditional reading, see b(i)).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Test the validity of a(i) above by means of a Venn diagram. (2 x 2 marks)
(ii) Using EAO-3 syllogism in a(i) above, construct an enthymeme of the third order. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Venn diagram test.**

Draw three overlapping circles $S$ (pedagogues), $P$ (G.C.E Examiners) and $M$ (chiefs); the eight regions are named by the circles they lie in. Shade a region to show that it is empty; the premises are drawn first and the conclusion must be read off the diagram without any further marking.

*Camestres (AEE-2).* "All $P$ are $M$" shades the part of $P$ outside $M$; "No $S$ are $M$" shades the part of $S$ inside $M$.

| Region | Shaded by |
|:-|:-|
| $P$ only | All $P$ are $M$ |
| $S \cap P$ only (outside $M$) | All $P$ are $M$ |
| $S \cap M$ only (outside $P$) | No $S$ are $M$ |
| $S \cap P \cap M$ | No $S$ are $M$ |

The overlap of $S$ and $P$ is made of the regions "$S \cap P$ only" and "$S \cap P \cap M$": both are shaded. The conclusion "No $S$ are $P$" is therefore shown by the premises alone: **the syllogism is valid**.

*Felapton (EAO-3).* "No $M$ are $P$" shades $M \cap P$ (the regions "$P \cap M$ only" and "$S \cap P \cap M$"); "All $M$ are $S$" shades the part of $M$ outside $S$ (the regions "$M$ only" and "$P \cap M$ only"). The only part of $M$ left unshaded is "$S \cap M$ only" (inside $S$, outside $P$).

The conclusion "Some $S$ are not $P$" needs an element in $S$ outside $P$ (regions "$S$ only" or "$S \cap M$ only"). The diagram of the two universal premises does not put an X there. Two readings:

- With the traditional (Aristotelian) assumption that the class $M$ (chiefs) is not empty, the only unshaded region of $M$ receives the X, and this region lies in $S$ outside $P$: the conclusion follows and **Felapton is valid** (valid by existential import).
- With the modern (Boolean) reading, where universal propositions carry no existential import, nothing forces an X into those regions: the same form is **invalid**.

Since the question uses the traditional mood names, the answer expected is that both syllogisms are valid, Felapton conditionally on the existence of chiefs.

**(ii) Enthymeme of the third order.**

An enthymeme is a syllogism with one proposition left unexpressed. In the traditional classification an enthymeme of the first order omits the major premise, one of the second order omits the minor premise, and one of the **third order omits the conclusion**. From the EAO-3 syllogism:

> No chiefs are G.C.E Examiners, and all chiefs are pedagogues.

(The conclusion "Some pedagogues are not G.C.E Examiners" is left to be understood by the hearer.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Using the major premise of the AEE-2 argument above, give the converse of its obverse. (3 marks)
(ii) Given that the proposition: "No illiterates are scholars" is False, state the truth value of its subaltern, contradictory and contrary respectively. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Converse of the obverse of the major premise.**

Major premise of the AEE-2 argument: "All G.C.E Examiners are chiefs" (A).

- Obverse (change the quality, replace the predicate by its complement): **No G.C.E Examiners are non-chiefs** (E).
- Converse (interchange subject and predicate; an E proposition converts simply): **No non-chiefs are G.C.E Examiners.**

**(ii) Truth values when "No illiterates are scholars" (E) is false.**

| Relation | Proposition | Truth value | Reason |
|:-|:-|:-:|:-|
| Subaltern | "Some illiterates are not scholars" (O) | Doubtful | The truth of a universal gives the truth of its subaltern, but the falsity of a universal leaves the particular undetermined |
| Contradictory | "Some illiterates are scholars" (I) | **True** | Contradictories always have opposite truth values |
| Contrary | "All illiterates are scholars" (A) | Doubtful | Contraries cannot both be true but can both be false; the falsity of E leaves A open |

**Answer:** subaltern: doubtful; contradictory: true; contrary: doubtful.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Translate the following disjunctive proposition into a hypothetical proposition: Either the state is ruled by the present ruling party or the opposition takes over. (2 marks)
(ii) Using d (i) above construct a valid Modus Tollens. (2 marks)
(iii) Construct a fallacy of 'ad hominem.' (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) From a disjunction to a hypothetical proposition.**

Let $R$ = the state is ruled by the present ruling party; $O$ = the opposition takes over. "Either $R$ or $O$" is equivalent to "if not $R$, then $O$":

**If the state is not ruled by the present ruling party, then the opposition takes over.** ($\sim R \supset O$)

(An equivalent form is "If the opposition does not take over, then the state is ruled by the present ruling party": $\sim O \supset R$.)

**(ii) A valid Modus Tollens** (denying the consequent of a hypothetical premise to deny its antecedent):

> If the state is not ruled by the present ruling party, then the opposition takes over.
> The opposition does not take over.
> Therefore, the state is ruled by the present ruling party.

Form: $\sim R \supset O,\ \sim O\ \therefore\ \sim\sim R$, that is $R$ by double negation. Valid (verified by truth table).

**(iii) A fallacy of ad hominem** (rejecting a claim by attacking the person who makes it, not the reasons):

> Mr Ayuk says that the school canteen should sell only fresh food. Nobody should listen to him, because he is a lazy man who was sacked from his last job.

This is fallacious: whether the canteen should sell fresh food depends on health and cost, not on Mr Ayuk's character or work record, so his personal faults do not refute his proposal.
